title: Calcium imaging and BAPTA loading of amygdala astrocytes in mouse brain slices
protocol: Transfer the slices into an aCSF filled recording chamber connected to a peristaltic pump that provides continuous flow of oxygenated aCSF (∼2 mL/min) at room temperature (or any temperature as needed by the experiment).
Place a holding harp on top of the slice to prevent movement.
Ensure the strings of the harp are not too close to the recording site.
Use an Axio examiner Zeiss microscope with a 4× objective to identify the region of interest.
Set the microscope to infrared differential interference contrast (IR-DIC, λ = 750–790nm).
Visualize the image with uEye cockpit software.
Switch to a 40× water-immersion objective and find the surface of the slice.
Open MetaFluor software and click the “Configure” menu.
Set spinning disk pinhole diameter to 70 μm.
Set spinning disk rotation speed to 15,000 rpm.
Set wavelength to 575 nm for SR101 and 475 nm for OGB.
Set exposure time to 20 ms for SR101 and 80 ms for OGB.
Set illumination intensity to 220 μW for SR101 and 580 μW for OGB.
Set sampling frequency to 2 Hz (500 ms interval between acquisitions).
Before switching on the fluorescent light, ensure the microscope is in confocal mode.
Start at an illumination intensity of 0 μW and an illumination time of 20 ms.
Progressively increase both the illumination intensity and time.
Set the illumination intensity between 580 μW and 1040 μW.
Use an illumination time of 20 ms for good OGB1 loading.
Never illuminate more than 100 ms.
Find a focal plane that includes several astrocytes labeled with SR101.
Check the shape of the cells: a healthy cell must have a ramified morphology with observable proximal processes.
Observe cells labeled with both SR101 and OGB, indicating astrocytes well loaded with both indicators.
Identify SR101 negative cells as probably being neurons.
Note cells labeled with SR101 but OGB1 negative.
Adjust the focal plane to see the cell and distinguish proximal processes.
Click on “Save pictures” and choose an appropriate folder.
Click on “Zero clock” and then “Start”.
Record data as independent pictures in the selected folder for 10 minutes.
Ensure a sampling frequency of at least twice the maximal frequency of the events recorded.
Use a 2 Hz sampling frequency for somatic global calcium transients lasting more than 2 seconds.
Apply TGOT at 1 nM for 10 seconds through the perfusion system.
Discard the solution for approximately 5 minutes if using a closed-loop perfusion aCSF to avoid contamination of the clean aCSF stock.

Transfer the slices into an aCSF filled recording chamber connected to a peristaltic pump that provides a continuous flow of oxygenated aCSF (∼2 mL/min) at room temperature (or any temperature as needed by the experiment).
Identify your region of interest using an Axio examiner Zeiss microscope with a 4× objective.
Set the microscope to infrared differential interference contrast (IR-DIC, λ = 750–790 nm) and visualize the image with uEye cockpit software or equivalent.
Switch to a 40× water-immersion objective and find the surface of the slice.
Visualize the cells with infrared illumination to verify that the slice is healthy.
Check for dead cells which can be discriminated by their round shape and absence of clear edges.
Visualize SR101 labeled astrocytes by illuminating the slice with yellow ∼575 nm light.
Identify the cell you want to patch without adjusting the microscopic stage position in either the x or y-axes.
Raise the objective far away from the slice, keeping the lens submerged in the solution.
Take a pulled pipette previously filled with the internal solution.
Place a pipetman tip on a 1 mL syringe to create a pipette filler.
Heat and pull the tip until it is thin enough to enter the pipette.
Blow air into the tip while pulling to avoid clogging.
Use a razor blade to cut the end of the pulled tip.
Verify that the tip is not blocked by pushing water through it.
Insert the pipette onto the AgCl electrode.
Apply positive pressure (about 1 mL of air with a syringe).
Position the pipette in the bath using the manipulator.
Use the membrane test in pClamp to determine pipette resistance (if signal drifts, see troubleshooting).
Apply a voltage step of 5–10 mV in voltage-clamp and measure current transients to calculate pipette’s resistance using Ohm’s law.
Ensure pipette resistance is ∼6 ± 2 MΩ (see troubleshooting for details).
Under infrared light, bring the pipette tip under the objective using the micromanipulator.
Move the pipette along x and y axes until a shadow appears on the screen.
Adjust the objective to focus on the shadow.
Position the pipette tip in focus.
Monitor both computer screen and actual pipette to avoid hitting obstacles.
Once pipette is in bath, move it carefully along z-axis to lower just above the slice.
Lower the objective.
Lower the pipette until you can see it again.
Repeat this sequence until just above the tissue slice.
Position the pipette tip above the targeted cell, slightly to its side.
Switch the microscope channel to view fluorescent labeling of astrocytes.
Lower the pipette into the tissue until on the same level as the target cell's top.
Move the pipette toward the cell.
Approach the cell diagonally for easier positioning.
Observe a visible deflection (dimple) on the membrane under positive pressure.
Expect an increase in pipette resistance of about 0.2 MΩ–1 MΩ when close to the cell.
Release the positive pressure to observe increased resistance as more membrane enters the pipette.
Apply positive pressure until the resistance reaches 15-20 MΩ when releasing it.
Hold the potential at -80 mV after reaching 100 MΩ to facilitate gigaseal formation.
Gently apply negative pressure by mouth until achieving a gigaseal (several GΩ).
Open the membrane gently using repetitive suction once a gigaseal is reached.
Switch to current-clamp mode to check the resting membrane potential after calcium imaging.
Apply current steps of 15 increments starting at −100 pA and increasing by 50 pA, each lasting 100 ms.
Wait 20 minutes for BAPTA to diffuse into the astrocyte network.
Monitor access resistance regularly during the experiment.
Remove the pipette very slowly and carefully along the x-axis.
Repeat all steps from patching another astrocyte located approximately one screen (200 μm) apart.
